question_text: According to the course material, GST201: Nigerian Peoples and Culture is a:
option_a: one-semester 2-credit unit course made up of 14 units
option_c: postgraduate seminar with no study units
explanation: The course guide states GST201 is a one-semester 2-credit unit course made up of 14 units.

question_text: According to the course material, the overall aim of GST201 is to introduce you to:
option_a: the history of traditional Nigerian peoples and culture
explanation: The overall aim of GST201 is to introduce you to the history of traditional Nigerian peoples and culture.

question_text: According to the course material, among several others, at least six major ethnic groups in Southern Nigeria include the Yoruba, the Bini, the Igbo, and:
option_a: the Itsekiri, the Urhobo and the Ijaw
option_b: the Inuit, the Maori and the Sami
explanation: The material identifies at least six major Southern groups: Yoruba, Bini, Igbo, Itsekiri, Urhobo and Ijaw.

question_text: According to the course material, Unit 1 of Module 1 focuses mainly on which three Southern peoples?
option_a: the Yoruba, the Bini and the Igbo
option_b: the Tiv, the Jukun and the Igala
option_c: the Fulani, the Tuareg and the Berber
option_d: the Efik, the Ibibio and the Kanuri only
explanation: Unit 1 deals with the Yoruba, the Bini and the Igbo as the first three major Southern groups.

question_text: According to the course material, the Yoruba ethnic group is believed to have come into existence between:
explanation: The material states the Yoruba ethnic group is believed to have come into existence between 2000-1000 BC.

question_text: According to Rev. Samuel Johnson's version cited in the course material, the Yoruba originally came from:
option_a: the North-Eastern area of Africa
option_b: Iceland via the Atlantic slave squadron
explanation: Johnson traces the origin of the Yoruba to the East / North-Eastern area of Africa.

question_text: According to the course material, Oduduwa is believed to be the first leader that led the Yoruba to:
option_a: Ile-Ife and subsequently sent his sons and grandsons to found other Yoruba kingdoms
option_b: Kano city as the Hausa Bokwoi capital
explanation: Oduduwa is believed to have led the Yoruba to Ile-Ife and sent sons and grandsons to found other kingdoms.

question_text: According to the Oke Oramfe version in the course material, after Obatala got drunk with palm wine:
option_a: Oduduwa seized the symbol of authority and eventually led the party to the world
option_b: the British amalgamated Northern and Southern Nigeria
option_c: Bayajida killed the snake at Daura well
explanation: Obatala got drunk; Oduduwa seized the symbol of authority and led the party to the world.

question_text: According to the course material, Oyo Empire was founded in the middle of the fifteenth century by:
option_a: Oranmiyan, the son of Oduduwa
explanation: Various traditions believe Oyo was founded by Oranmiyan, the son of Oduduwa.

question_text: According to the course material, the Alaafin was assisted and regulated by the Oyomesi, a council of:
option_a: seven members headed by Bashorun who acted as the prime minister
option_b: forty-four emirs headed by the Mai of Bornu
option_d: village Okparas headed by the Ofo
explanation: The Oyomesi was a council of seven members headed by Bashorun who acted as prime minister.

question_text: According to the course material, the Ogboni cult played a mediatory role in any conflict between:
option_a: the Oyomesi and the Alaafin
option_c: the Mai of Bornu and Bayajida
option_d: the Attah of Igala and Achadu only
explanation: The Ogboni cult played a mediatory role in any conflict between the Oyomesi and the Alaafin.

question_text: According to the course material, the head of the traditional Yoruba army was conferred with the title of:
option_a: Are-Ona-Kankanfo
explanation: The army head was conferred with the coveted title of Are-Ona-Kankanfo.

question_text: According to the course material, Unit 2 of Module 1 focuses on the last three major ethnic groups of Southern Nigeria, namely:
option_a: the Itsekiri, the Urhobo and the Ijaw
option_b: the Hausa, the Kanem-Bornu and the Nupe
option_c: the Igala, the Jukun and the Tiv
option_d: the Yoruba, the Bini and the Igbo
explanation: Unit 2 focuses on the Itsekiri, the Urhobo and the Ijaw.

question_text: According to the course material, Unit 3 of Module 1 focuses on the first three major ethnic groups of Northern Nigeria, namely:
option_a: the Hausa, the Kanem-Bornu and the Nupe
option_b: the Yoruba, the Bini and the Igbo
option_c: the Itsekiri, the Urhobo and the Ijaw
option_d: the Igala, the Jukun and the Tiv
explanation: Unit 3 focuses on the Hausa, the Kanem-Bornu and the Nupe.

question_text: According to the course material, at least six major ethnic groups in Northern Nigeria include the Hausa, the Kanem-Bornu, the Nupe, and:
option_a: the Igala, the Jukun and the Tiv
option_b: the Yoruba, the Bini and the Igbo
option_c: the Itsekiri, the Ijaw and the Urhobo
option_d: the Efik, the Ibibio and the Anang only
explanation: The six named Northern groups are Hausa, Kanem-Bornu, Nupe, Igala, Jukun and Tiv.

question_text: According to the course material, most scholars agree that the most authentic oral tradition explaining the origin of the Hausa states is:
option_a: the Bayajida story
explanation: Most scholars agree that the Bayajida story is the most authentic oral tradition explaining Hausa origins.

question_text: According to the Bayajida legend in the course material, after helping to kill a snake at a well in Daura, Bayajida married the queen and they had a son named:
option_a: Bawo
explanation: Bayajida and the queen of Daura later had a son named Bawo.

question_text: According to the course material, Bawo's six children together with Bayajida's other son at Biran are believed to have founded:
option_a: the original seven Hausa states referred to as the Hausa Bokwoi
explanation: They founded the original seven Hausa states referred to as the Hausa Bokwoi.

question_text: According to the course material, by the year 2000 the Hausa population was estimated at about:
option_a: twenty million
explanation: By the year 2000, the Hausa population was estimated at about twenty million.

question_text: According to the course material, Idah has always been known as the capital state of:
option_a: Igala people
explanation: Idah has always been known as the capital state of Igala people.

question_text: According to the course material, Abutu Eje, sometimes identified as a child reared by a leopard or as a prince from Ado (Benin) or Apa (Wukari Jukun), contributed to the evolution of:
option_a: the Igala state
explanation: Abutu Eje was the first personality to seriously contribute to the development of the Igala state.

question_text: According to the course material, some Igala elites attribute the emergence of their state to Achadu, believed to have come from:
option_a: the Igbo country
explanation: Achadu is believed to have come from the Igbo country.

question_text: According to the course material, Unit 4 of Module 1 focuses on the last three Northern groups, namely:
option_a: the Igala, the Jukun or Kwararafa and the Tiv
option_b: the Yoruba, the Bini and the Igbo
option_c: the Itsekiri, the Urhobo and the Ijaw
option_d: the Hausa, the Nupe and the Kanem-Bornu
explanation: Unit 4 focuses on the Igala, the Jukun or Kwararafa and the Tiv.

question_text: According to the course material, there are no compulsory pre-requisites for GST201.
option_a: True: the course guide states there are no compulsory pre-requisites
option_b: False: students must first pass CSC 103
option_c: False: only Criminology students may register
option_d: False: a laboratory science credit is required
explanation: The course guide states there are no compulsory pre-requisites for this course.

question_text: According to the course material, Nzemeke and Erhagbe (2002), Nigerian Peoples and Culture (2nd ed.), is:
option_a: the first recommended textbook and is compulsory for this course
explanation: The first recommended textbook is compulsory: Nzemeke and Erhagbe (2002).
